speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WELCOME TO YUGOSLAV FOREIGN MINISTER AND WIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon it is my privilege to say a few words of welcome to Hon. Koca Popovic, the foreign minister of Yugoslavia, and Mrs. Popovic, who are visiting in Ottawa for a day or two.
As hon. members know, Mr. Popovic represents a country which has shown great courage and great steadfastness, and which has been our ally in two world wars. Both the foreign minister and his wife were officers in the partisan army. The minister eventually became the commander in chief of that force, and both had very distinguished careers in those trying days.
Since the war the minister has taken a very active part in the work of the United Nations, where his country has stood for peace and has always taken a stand which would lead in that direction. Yugoslavia, like Canada, is one of the middle powers of the world today, and one of the powers which depends so much on an effective world organization.
It is very significant that in far-away Palestine there are several hundred young Yugoslav soldiers serving beside approximately the same number of young Canadians in the United Nations emergency force. They have been participating together there now for some years, making a great contribution, which I think sometimes Canadians are inclined to forget.
Therefore, under all these conditions it is a very happy occasion for me to be able to welcome the minister and his wife to Canada and in particular to the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WELCOME TO YUGOSLAV FOREIGN MINISTER AND WIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the opposition I should like to associate ourselves with the welcome which has been expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the foreign minister of Yugoslavia and his wife. We welcome them, Mr. Speaker, not only on their own behalf but because the foreign minister represents a country which in the past has fought fearlessly for its freedom against all aggressors, and we know it will continue to do so in the future.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the need for the Canadian government to remove the present state of confusion in the uranium industry by making an immediate statement of policy that will assure the Canadian uranium industry, and employees engaged therein, of (a) minimum quantities of uranium that it will insist shall be purchased by Britain as a result of the commitment made for purchase of uranium during the period April, 1963 to December 31, 1966; (b) the general basis of allocation of the market within the industry; (c) the maintenance of uranium communities such as Uranium City, Elliot Lake, Bancroft.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If I understand the hon. member's request, it is to interrupt our proceedings under rule 26 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, and that the matter of urgent public importance is the need for a statement of policy by the government with respect to the uranium industry?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. With respect to the question of urgency, we believe there is a great state of confusion in the uranium industry in our country at this time that has not been cleared up by the statements made in the house yesterday, and this confusion is brought about because of the uncertainty in the public mind with regard to the quantities of uranium that will be sold under the contract, or under the commitment

Inquiries of the Ministry made between Canada and the United Kingdom. By this motion we are asking as a matter of urgency that the government should state to the country now the immediate quantities of uranium that the Canadian government will insist that Britain purchase from Canada on the basis of the commitment to which the Prime Minister has referred. After that has been stated there should be some indication of the general basis of allocation of this market within the industry in Canada so the various components of the industry will know their economic position and, further, so the uranium communities in Canada such as Uranium City, Elliot Lake, Bancroft and others will be assured that they will be maintained over this period.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think it is unnecessary to consider the matter further. It seems to me that the hon. member's interest in this matter should be expressed at a time provided by the general rules of the house rather than in a special debate under rule 26 which would interrupt all other proceedings. My view that this matter does not come strictly within the rule is based partly on the sittings of a committee of the house which has this matter before it and where there is ample opportunity to inquire into and deal with the problem of uranium supplies and marketing. In fact I think the issue has come to the fore through that committee which has not yet reported.
Furthermore, from listening to the discussion of this matter in the house it appears that the main controversy is over the sale of uranium to the United Kingdom between the years 1963 and 1966. Therefore it seems to me that parliament will have ample opportunity to deal comprehensively with this important matter in the course of its ordinary proceedings and at the usual time.

690.	Contribution towards the costs of a special meeting of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations regarding distribution and use of fish meal, $2,500.

On this item I should like to lodge a complaint with the minister, with the Department of Fisheries and with the government as a whole. In recent years we have received notice of a developing practice, especially on the part of fishing companies located in British Columbia, under which, in the production of herring fish meal, they are moving into other countries and using their capital resources, taking advantage of lower labour costs, especially in such countries as Peru, to develop large herring fishing industries. This has the result of undercutting and eliminating the Canadian production of fish meal, and consequently our herring fishermen have had to suffer long months of unemployment. They have now been re-employed at reduced rates. Their income has been reduced because of the activities of Canadian corporations which are establishing herring fishing enterprises in other countries.
These corporations are using Canadian resources to do this. They are using the profits they made in Canada in the Latin American and South American countries, with the result -I will not say with the purpose-that many Canadians interested in herring fishing, and who have invested their whole life savings in gear and equipment, are either unemployed or have their income reduced. If we are to engage in international aid in regard to the distribution of fish meal, I feel that Canadian fish meal should be distributed to those nations in the world that have need of it. Consequently every consideration ought to be given to the Canadian production of fish meal, and we should not be voting money here that will help to distribute to the needy nations of the world the fish meal that has been produced by Canadian corporations in countries other than Canada. If we are to give aid in this respect we ought to ensure that Canadian fishermen get the benefit, and that we are not

actually aiding Canadian corporations in their profit-making schemes in other countries of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat a question I asked the Minister of Justice on March 7 and I quote now from page 1798 of Hansard:
I should like to direct a question to the Acting Minister of Justice. In view of the fines levied on eight electrical companies in the United States for bid rigging and price fixing, will the minister tell the house whether any investigation is being made or is contemplated by the combines investigation branch into similar practices by the Canadian counterparts of these electrical companies?
The Solicitor General, who was the acting minister of justice at that time, said:
I will take this question as notice and give the member an answer at an early date.
If the answer has been given I have missed it. I wonder whether the minister can throw any light on this question.

Mr. Chairman, I do not imagine that the Minister of Finance could be expected to reply to that question, but I rise with a similar purpose in mind. On March 13 I asked a question in similar vein with respect to combines administration. My question referred to two articles that had appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail under the by-line of Mr. Bruce Macdonald in which it was alleged that since the passing of legislation last session electrical goods were no longer available except at prices 25 per cent to 40 per cent higher than had been normal prior to last year's legislation coming into effect. At that time the parliamentary secretary replied to my question in these words, as found on page 2914 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the officials are on the job in this respect, but I shall be glad to refer the matter to the appropriate officials for comment.

I have been very intrigued this afternoon to note the lack of co-operation that the Minister of Finance is experiencing so far as his colleagues are concerned when he is called upon to deal with problems of this nature in this important committee of supply. We have only been in committee for about 20 minutes. I saw the Minister of Justice conveniently retire, but I thought fortunately we still had his parliamentary secretary here. However, as we approached closer to the items under the heading "Justice", by coincidence or otherwise the parliamentary secretary retired. Then I thought that we were still all right because the Solicitor General, who has acted as minister of justice, was with us and perhaps we would be able to get some information from him on these matters about which we could not expect the Minister of Finance to have complete details. However, as we were getting closer and closer to the items under the heading "Justice", off went the Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He cleared out, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, any connection between the particular items now engaging the attention of the committee and the movement of my colleagues and the hon. members to whom reference has been made is, I am quite certain, purely coincidental. The long-time practice of the house has been that the final supplementaries coming at the close of the fiscal year are handled by the Minister of Finance as best he can. I may say that I do not find the lack of co-operation on the part of my colleagues that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River professes to find.
So far as the question of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo is concerned, I shall be glad to draw his inquiry to the attention of my colleague.

Can the minister tell us the number of prosecutions under this legislation in the fiscal year just ending compared with the number in the previous fiscal year and also whether the change, if any, is responsible for the increased expenditure?

I am delighted to see that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice was only behind the curtain and is now back in his seat. I refer to him the question I posed as long ago as March 13 last. It related to allegations that under the new combines legislation passed last session electrical consumer goods are no longer available generally throughout the country except at prices 25 per cent to 40 per cent higher than those prevailing prior to the new legislation. In my view this confirmed the warning of

the opposition last year when the legislation was introduced. We asserted then that such legislation was likely to have a very adverse effect upon consumers. We pointed in the strongest possible terms the danger of price fixing, particularly if jurisdiction over price fixing was to be removed from the Department of Justice and, as is usually the case under Conservative administrations, transferred to the hands of powerful manufacturers such as Canadian General Electric and others who are referred to in the articles by Mr. Bruce Macdonald in the Globe and Mail.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to say for the record that there is no evidence whatsoever that the consumer has been harmed in any way by the legislation enacted last year. In fact I think the contrary is the case. I am not sure whether the hon. member wants a specific answer at this time to the question he posed.

The parliamentary secretary will recall that he assured me that after consulting the officials he would furnish some information to the house. These articles received considerable prominence, and my recollection is that they asserted facts in a most positive way. They referred to companies, they referred to products, and they referred to very distinct changes in consumer prices in the range I have already mentioned and which I referred to in my question of March 13 to which no reply has yet been made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on March 13 was as follows:
Would the parliamentary secretary inquire and inform the house whether officials have examined the first retail pricing guide issued by the Canadian General Electric Company Limited after the government's amendments to the Combines Investigation Act last session to ascertain whether consumer electrical goods, in consequence, are no longer available except at prices 25 per cent to 40 per cent higher than formerly?
If an examination has taken place, is the minister satisfied that because of the amendments of last session there is no offence against the remaining provisions of the act respecting resale price maintenance?
In reply to this question I may say the matter has been brought to the attention of the director and is presently being examined to determine whether an inquiry is warranted. Of course, as the hon. member knows, the general practice is not to give out information on whether or not an inquiry is proceeding unless and until a report is published.

Mr. Chairman, I agree that the government needs this additional amount. I believe a useful purpose is served in exposing the activities of Canadian or other corporations in so far as price fixing is concerned. However, in a certain way we are simply pouring 90205-6-216J
Supply-Justice
money down the drain. Almost every major industry in Canada has been found guilty of violating the Combines Investigation Act, yet no beneficial results have flowed to the Canadian consumer except the publicity given to these matters. I feel the time is rapidly approaching when the Canadian government should reconsider its position in connection with this subject.
I remember very well indeed, Mr. Chairman, when our present Prime Minister was a member of the opposition. At that time he demanded of the government of the day that the Combines Investigation Act be amended in order to put some teeth into it. It was his contention then that anyone who was found guilty of violating the Combines Investigation Act, no matter how high ranking an officer he might be, should have imposed on him a mandatory term behind bars. He ought to have to go to jail, because the mere levying of a fine is ineffective and even ludicrous. If the Prime Minister meant what he said a few weeks ago, that the issue in the next election is going to be free enterprise versus socialism, I believe his election appeal is going to meet with very little response unless he is able to show that his government really believes in free enterprise.
We have had all these investigations in the past, and almost without exception Canadian enterprise has been found guilty of plotting and scheming in an unethical way, in an illegal way, to rob the consumers. Even the Minister of Finance, I believe it was in his budget address in 1959, admitted to this house the concern of the government over the growing power of corporations to determine prices regardless of the normal laws of supply and demand. If the election issue is going to be free enterprise versus socialism, the government will have to convince the Canadian people that there is some free enterprise.
I happened to be in the United States at the time the officials of the electrical industry were convicted of combining. I can assure the minister that after these officials were sentenced to jail the people of the United States found a renewed faith in the fundamentals of free enterprise. We have seen nothing of the kind happen in Canada. I think we ought to take the Prime Minister's advice when, as an opposition member, he advocated that if our Canadian people are to be expected to believe in the existence of free enterprise, if they are not to become cynical, then we will have to prove by the implementation of the Combines Investigation Act that we mean what we say. After all, Mr. Chairman, I do not see why a man who steals a bit of wire from the B.C. Electric should be sentenced to two years in the penitentiary, while a man

Supply-Justice
who is a member of the baking industry combine and who needlessly adds one cent per loaf to the cost of every loaf of bread the Canadian housewife buys, should only be fined. In my opinion the baker is a bigger criminal than the man who steals a bit of wire from his employer.
I would urge upon the government that they look at the attitude and the thinking of the government across the border in connection with this issue, and recall how quickly the confidence of the people of the United States was restored in the institution of government. In contrast, our government merely carries on year after year by levying fines upon those who have been found guilty. This means nothing to these people. As a matter of fact they very often increase their rate of violation immediately after the results of an inquiry have been released.
If the minister is really concerned about the growing power of Canadian corporations to determine price levels regardless of the normal law of supply and demand, I recommend that before we vote much more money to the combines investigation branch we consider amending this act so that it will have some effect on the Canadian economy and on the faith the Canadian people are supposed to have in our method of doing business, as well as upon the respect our people are supposed to have for law and order in this country.

Mr. Chairman, we should hear something from the minister on this subject. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice told us a few minutes ago there was no evidence that prices had been increased since the change was made in the legislation last year. Obviously the parliamentary secretary has not been shopping recently or he would know from his own experience that prices for many lines of hard goods have increased. The Minister of Finance should be interested in this matter, because the Minister of Finance is interested in the total amount of business done in this country and in the total number of jobs available to Canadian workers.
The Minister of Finance is well aware of the fact that there is an elastic demand for many of these hard goods. The lower the price is, the greater the market, and the greater the market the more jobs there are for the people who manufacture these goods. Part of the trouble with our economy at the present time is this matter of the rigidities which are being built into it. One of these rigidities is fixed prices. I think the minister should look into the effects of the changes in the legislation which were enacted by parliament last year to determine the extent to which they have caused prices to be increased, as well as the effect this has had on markets

and consequently upon employment in Canada. I think he should do this not only for his own sake but because he has a responsibility to this House of Commons and to the Canadian people because of his high office.
The productivity council should look at it also.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 696 carry?

No. I should not like this opportunity to go by without making this comment. When I referred to the budget contribution of the Minister of Finance in 1959 I noted that he, by shaking his head, attempted to deny that he had indicated as I mentioned. I should like to read to the minister what he had to say as reported at page 2408 of Hansard of April 9, 1959 when, among other things, he said this:
Advancing technology might have been expected to reduce the cost and selling price of many products to consumers. It is evident, however, that developments in corporation pricing policies, in labour organization and even in our political democracy are producing increased rigidities which inhibit the free play of competitive forces and thereby promote inflation and price increases.
All I am asking at this time is what are the intentions of the government with regard to this concern so aptly and ably expressed by the minister on April 9, 1959, other than a mere pouring of more money into more investigations that will find even more Canadian corporations guilty, but will have no effect in reality except to build up an attitude of despair and cynicism on the part of Canadian consumers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am obliged to the hon. member for reading exactly what I did say in the budget speech of 1959 and in that way exposing his earlier misinterpretation of what I said in this regard. Hon. members are now in a position to contrast what I actually did say with the interpretation put upon it by the hon. member in his earlier remarks.
May I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that item 696 is for a further amount required in addition to a sum already voted by parliament and to be found in the Appropriation Act passed earlier in the session of 1960. In this situation, as I understand it, the rule that applies is that we are not debating the principle of the main item but are simply endeavouring to decide whether the additional amount now proposed is in fact required.
I may say that this additional amount is in fact required. It is required owing to an unforeseen increase in reporting costs and other fees and expenses in unusually prolonged inquiries, and to cover the cost of travelling to hearings at points outside of Ottawa. These are additional expenses necessarily incurred

in the effective enforcement of our combines legislation. I would have thought that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would warmly applaud these demonstrated efforts at effective enforcement of the legislation enacted by parliament in this regard.

I want to say just one word. Surely we are in order in discussing here the government's schizophrenic approach to the matter of combines. On the one hand it spends more money on prolonged investigations, and on the other hand it introduces legislation which is responsible for more prolonged investigations owing to the fact that it enables companies to have broader scope in the fixing of prices within the law. For this reason we are perfectly justified in questioning further expenditures which might not have been necessary if the government had not taken an altogether different position in the legislation it placed before this House of Commons last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 696 carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. The minister made an attempt to indicate that we might even be out of order. No one here attempted to debate the principle of the Combines Investigation Act. We only ask the government, before we vote the additional amount for the implementation of this act, what its intentions are in this regard.
I listened carefully to the hon. member for Trinity when he spoke previously, and he also complained about the rigidity in our price structure. I indicated the minister's complaint on April 9, 1959 about the rigidity in our price structure. All I am asking of the minister is that he indicate what intentions the government has in this regard. Is this money now being asked for going to help to eliminate or to elasticize the rigidity that now exists by restoring a bit of old fashioned, honest, free enterprise into our economy?

I was going on to say that, following the statement which the Minister of Labour made and which can be found at page 6823 of Hansard of July 23, 1960, reference was made to seasonal unemployment and the assistance that was being given to combat seasonal unemployment by the winter works program. The government has attempted to deal with the matter on every opportunity which has been given in the house. The government has taken full credit for the creation of new jobs during the season of unemployment. To the extent that any new jobs have resulted from works provided by the government to relieve seasonal unemployment, in my opinion and that of those of us who sit on this side of the house credit should go to the local authorities on whom the major financial burden of these projects has fallen.
On July 23 of last year the Minister of Labour stated that the average labour content of all municipal winter works is 34.5 per cent. As the committee knows, the federal government pays 50 per cent of the direct labour cost or approximately 17 per cent of the total cost. An additional 25 per cent to 40 per cent of the direct labour cost is borne by the province. In the case of the province of Quebec 40 per cent of those costs are being paid by that government, and were it not for what is being done by way of assistance with regard to seasonal unemployment in the province of Quebec, unemployment there would be much higher than it is. The point I am trying to make is that under this scheme

Supply-Labour
for combating seasonal unemployment the main burden falls upon the municipalities.
I have compiled here two tables which indicate that the winter works program is not as effective in its impact as the government would have us believe. Special table 3(c) breaks down the labour force estimates of employment by industry and by occupation, and I should like to table a compilation of figures derived from special table (c) entitled "Employed by Industry and Occupation" issued by the special surveys division of the dominion bureau of statistics. I should like to ask permission to table these two documents.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If hon. members would look at the first table entitled "Employment in Construction Industry" they would see there were 10,000 fewer jobs in construction in February of this year than there were in January, and 24,000 fewer than in February, 1960. Thus, the winter works program has not mitigated the seasonal decline in employment in the construction industry between January and February.
In so far as the other table is concerned *-the table entitled "Employment by Occupation"-as can be seen from the table which has just been filed there was a decline of
4.000	workers in 1958, but during the last three years there has not been a decline in the number of what are termed construction workers between January and February. During 1959 there was an increase of some
5.000	workers and this year there was an increase between January and February of some 7,000 workers.
However, the point I am trying to make, and which is borne out by this latter table, is that the winter works program has had

no discernable impact on the employment of labourers and unskilled workers. There were approximately 21,000 fewer jobs in this occupational category in February of this year than in January. We have, of course, asked the government on a number of occasions-the hon. member for Essex East and others, too-for a local breakdown of the projects undertaken during this year's winter works program. We have not as yet obtained the answer, so we have been unable to analyse the local impact of the projects.
There are a few explanations why the government can claim that there were 105,000 additional jobs created by the program and why there has still been no amelioration of the seasonal unemployment problem among construction and unskilled workers. These reasons are, first, that municipalities have undertaken during winter construction work which would normally be done in summer in the belief that the extra cost involved would be more than compensated for by the participation payments of the federal government. To the extent that this is true, no

new jobs have been created but, rather, unemployment in wintertime has been replaced by unemployment in the summertime. This has been brought to the attention of the government not only during discussions this year but also last year when an indication was given to the Minister of Labour that in so far as seasonal unemployment is concerned many of the municipalities which undertook works simply postponed the works from summer to winter, the effect of which was simply to postpone unemployment in wintertime to unemployment in summertime.
The other point I should like to make is that communities suffering from a -high incidence of seasonal unemployment have found themselves incapable of participating in the winter works program to any great extent because of the high level of cyclical unemployment they have experienced this year and the encumbent financial burden of increased welfare payments. Communities such as the city of Ottawa, for instance, where there is not a high level of unemployment, have been able to take advantage of winter works projects to a greater extent than communities which really need them. This, I think, is a factor which should be taken into consideration with regard to this whole matter of seasonal unemployment.
There are two suggestions I should like to make and then I shall resume my seat. They are a repetition-and I think they need to be repeated-of suggestions which have already been advanced by those of us who sit on this side of the chamber. They are, first, the establishment of a municipal loan fund, and, second, the incorporation in the winter works program of a formula on a sliding scale of federal participation depending on the amount of unemployment in a particular area. That would have the effect of insuring that the winter works program had its- greatest impact in distressed areas. As a deterrent to seasonal unemployment and as a project to assist employment we do not think that what has been advanced by the government meets the situation at all, and now I have reference particularly to the formula which was brought down by the Minister of Labour having to do with accelerated depreciation. It is our opinion that the two suggestions I have just made would meet the situation far better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This item is one calling for the provision of a further amount of $65,000 to supplement the amount previously voted in the main estimates. It has nothing whatever to do with the municipal incentive winter works program. As I pointed out after the hon. member for Laurier had
Supply-Labour
launched into his remarks, this has to do with the effort made to encourage others than municipalities to undertake what measures may be open to them with a view to extending employment in the winter months. This is an offer that has been made by the Department of Labour, and with very encouraging results, to encourage people to do work in the winter and to undertake the job of creating work that can be done in winter months but is not always done then, for some reason or other.
This item is designed to provide the sums that have been expended for publicity in this regard, directed to bringing home to people their responsibilities in this respect, and the opportunities that do exist for the undertaking of work during the winter months. This lies completely outside the field of the municipal winter works incentive program. That is a matter that was undertaken, in so far as the estimates are concerned, under an item that was brought in with an earlier group of supplementary estimates. If we are going to have a debate on that I will be happy to participate in it but with respect, that lies completely outside the ambit of this present item.

In view of the remarks just made by the Minister of Finance, I take it that this involves some uncontemplated items of advertising and promotion that would have an ancillary effect with respect to the enlargement of the winter work. Perhaps it includes advertising such as I have here "Department of Labour-Do it Now with a Small Business Loan". Perhaps that is one of the items that was not contemplated when the main estimates were provided more than a year ago, and perhaps advertising of this kind would be provided for in the vote we have before us, is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That particular advertisement may have been included in the scope of the main original estimate. I cannot say precisely whether it was included in the sums provided for in the supplementary estimates now under consideration, but the increase that is provided for here, in the appropriation for this total purpose, arises in part out of the fact that after the main estimates were introduced in the house for the fiscal year 1960-61, the chartered banks indicated their willingness, when this matter was discussed with them, to service home improvement loans. This type of loan was extended by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to include the owners of rental properties. The winter employment committee within the Department of Labour recommended that, in view of the need to give

Supply-Labour
support to the promotion directed to home and farm improvement loans the increased cost for the printed material over the last year and the needed expansion to keep pace with demand, the expenditure for winter employment publicity should be increased. That has been approved and this additional sum of $65,000 resulted.
I was not referring to advertising with respect to home improvement loans because, after all, that has been a form of providing employment which has been in existence over a long number of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With respect, I think the hon. member is not right about that. The home improvement loans program was undertaken last autumn. What has been done in that respect since is quite additional to what has been done before. The co-operation of banks was enlisted and a new program was undertaken in this respect, and because this source is regarded as such a hopeful one for the provision of employment, a campaign was undertaken to promote the awareness on the part of Canadians of the fact that home improvement loans were available as well as farm improvement loans.

Farm improvement loans and home improvement loans arranged through the chartered banking system in this country have been available for years. There is nothing new in this regard except that the terms of the loans change from time to time as a result of the amendments regarding the amounts, and so on. I was referring to something that is new-small business loans-where again the enlistment of the chartered banks' support is made with the banks' numerous branches across the country. Since this legislation was passed it has been possible for businessmen to get small business loans. When this new legislation was introduced it was suggested that there was an accumulation of perhaps $65 million worth of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was $75 million.

Yes, $75 million-I stand corrected-of work that was standing ready and which would be accommodated under this new legislation. The minister will recall that I complained about this later, and said we thought, in order to assist the winter works emergency, this should have been advanced more rapidly. The opposition co-operated in this regard at the beginning and its debate and criticism were reduced to a minimum prior to Christmas. We were very surprised to find that the cabinet had not arranged

these regulations sufficiently in advance so that it would be possible, prior to January 19, for the banks in this country to be ready to receive applications for loans. Since that time a number of inquiries have been made regarding the approach to the target of this $75 million worth of work, to which the minister has referred, by the extension of loans. These were presumably requirements which were ready, on shelf.
A number of inquiries have been made in parliament of the Minister of Finance, because this was legislation initiated by him. It would seem that some of this money is required for advertising, through the Department of Labour, because we have seen advertisements across the country such as the one to which I referred-"Do it Now With a Small Business Loan". I am not referring to home or farm improvement loans, but new small business loans. Presumably because this is a new thing it could not have been provided in the main estimates which were prepared over a year ago. I do feel, however, that since January 19, 1961 when the cabinet's regulations were made public, the Minister of Finance has not been adequately communicative to this house and to the country with respect to progress under this new legislation.
I think on March 9 the hon. member for Port Arthur raised a question in respect of this subject and the reply of the minister was that there was no report available as yet. Later on March 22 the hon. member for Beauce asked what report of progress the minister could give.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was that not for January?

Yes, from January 19 to January 31 was the purport of his question. He asked how many loans had been made and what was the total amount involved. At that time the Minister of Finance said he had no information in that regard. I would suggest that while we are dealing with an item relating to the Minister of Labour, we are fortunate this time to have a direct tie-up with an item that appears to have been originally fathered by the Minister of Finance, and I think it is now time for the Minister of Finance to give us some information in a definite way as to the number and dollar volume of loans that had been made since January 19 under the small business loans legislation of this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The banks have 30 days to make returns in this respect. If the hon. member had read my answers to these questions instead of paraphrasing them he would have seen that what I had indicated was that if the starred question which was asked was rephrased to include the period

to February 28 I would be pleased to supply that information just as soon as it was available.
As I pointed out, there is no value in asking for a return for the last few days of the month of January because the loans only became available on January 19 and, after all, the processing had to be done after that.
In relation to the figure that has been quoted by the hon. member as to the work waiting to be done, in the discussion of this matter earlier in the session I used the figure of $75 million which, as I pointed out, had been furnished to me by the retail merchants' association of Canada as their estimate of the volume and value of work waiting to be done on retail premises in Canada in the modernization and reconstruction of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I pointed out that the additional amount required is attributable in part to the fact that the banks were persuaded last autumn to undertake the home improvement loan program, a substantial program, and it was considered most desirable in the interest of stimulating winter work that this fact should be brought to the attention of the Canadian public. This resulted in the enlargement of the expenditure for the publicity promotional program over that which was previously contemplated.
I may say that more and more companies, businesses, organizations, associations and all segments of society have been lending support to this campaign of persuading people to undertake as much of the job creating work as possible during wintertime, and have carried the winter work message in promotional media. This is a sample of the kind of co-operation that has been received by the Department of Labour from the public and is warmly appreciated. This has been made possible by the preparation of material by the Department of Labour, information branch, for non-government sources. This in itself has meant that more Canadians are being exposed to the idea of having more work done in the winter when men and materials are available, at a time when, quite apart from unemployment attributable to other causes, we have always had the problem of seasonal unemployment. It is estimated that for every dollar spent on paid advertisement by the government in this regard $10 has been contributed from outside sources. This includes, of course, not only national publicity but also local support which has greatly increased this year as a result of greater concentration across Canada by the local offices of the national employment service.

That is what I thought I understood the minister to say and I must admit I am surprised to have it confirmed to me. This government has endorsed some very strange principles. In many instances it has introduced what might be referred to as the Houdini system of accounting. The Minister of Public Works was asked in this house to consider the advisability of the chartered banks making loans at the current

Supply-Labour
National Housing Act rate. In reply, he said, with a certain amount of obvious righteousness, that the government would not consider tinkering with the bank rate; that it must continue the bank rate; that it must not allow a change to take place which would increase the charge to the Canadian taxpayers for loans made to them by the chartered banks; and he imputed political motives to us for making this suggestion.
And yet, Mr. Chairman, here we have the Minister of Finance doing the same thing by the back door method. Instead of allowing the chartered banks to increase their rates he says, "If you do what we ask you, we will do your advertising for you so that it will reduce your costs of doing business". This is a very strange principle, indeed.
The government refuses to face the fact that the banks will not make a certain type of loan at the rates which they are allowed to charge by law; but in order to encourage them to make the loans which the government wishes to have made the government says, "We will take some money out of our back pocket and we will do the advertising for you so that people will come to your doors and ask you for loans, and in this way we shall be mitigating the effect of the statutory limitation on the interest rates which you are allowed to charge." This is a most surprising thing, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance has done similar things with his obvious polish and sleight-of-hand in some of his bond savings campaigns. Therefore, he seeks to do by one indirect method what he refuses to do directly because of the political consequences of taking direct action.
Here we have the government of Canada spending the taxpayer's money to advertise private businesses, to advertise that private businesses are open to receive applications for business from the public at large. What principle could be more questionable than this one? I should like the Minister of Finance to explain to the committee why we should vote money to the government of Canada to enable it in effect to subsidize the rate of return which private institutions are able to obtain from the loans made to taxpayers who have to foot the bill for these expenditures on advertising.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the most ridiculous assertions, I think, that this committee has heard. I can only conclude that the hon. member has some animus toward the idea of having the banks launch with some vigour into a program of home improvement loans. I may say it was a matter of no little satisfaction to the government last autumn when, in discussion with the banks, we found the banks willing to 
undertake an invigorated program of home improvement loans. This obviously was going to be a source of employment particularly during the winter months because this is the type of work that can be carried on indoors.
If it is a justifiable policy on the part of the government to seek to increase employment during the winter months, then I should think it is not only equally justifiable but equally a duty of the government to see that as much use as possible is made of the facilities thus created. That is why, within the scope of the promotional program to which I have referred and which was provided by parliament in the main estimates for this purpose, the fact that the banks were providing home improvement loans was made known as one of many matters that indicated to people throughout the country that facilities existed making it desirable for them to undertake these job creating programs during the winter months.
This program has been successful because the expenditure of money on this promotional campaign has unquestionably had the effect of creating jobs, and it strikes me that this is hardly an occasion for a rebuke to be administered to the government by the hon. member. If it is the wish of hon. members that there should be no more unemployment than can be avoided and if it is the policy on the part of hon. members that work should be provided in the winter to meet the problem of seasonal unemployment, then I should think it would be the desire of hon. members to make this effective without dredging up accusations out of whole cloth, out of imagination, sheer fictional suggestion, that the government is trying to help the banks. In this situation the government is trying to help to provide employment.

Mr. Chairman, I did not expect much business acumen from the minister but surely he knows that any private business will spend its own money on advertising if it can engage in a venture which is profitable for it, and the mere fact that the government has to subsidize the banks is an indication that what they have been asked to do by the government would not otherwise be attractive to them.
If the minister is correct in his contention that it is legitimate for the government to advertise the particular services that are available, he can extend this principle to any field whatsoever. Surely if the government merely wishes to provide employment and is interested in doing so, it can subsidize any business. It can provide back door benefits to any business. That is precisely the objection, that this is a back door subsidy, a back door arrangement, back door

assistance rather than a forward approach so that the people of Canada will know the actual cost of the service they are receiving.
Here we have an instance where the banks will make loans at 6 per cent for home improvements while at the same time, according to the annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation distributed yesterday, they are not the least interested in making loans at the same interest rate for new housing. Why not? There must be some reason that the one is attractive to them while the other is not.
Surely one of the reasons is the fact that the minister has lifted from them the burden of servicing part of this particular business venture by reason of his assistance through the provision of free advertising. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to indicate the amount of free advertising he has provided on the basis of the different mass media listed in the details and also tell the committee whether any of this money was spent on advertising in the foreign language press of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the minister has been rather unfair to the hon. member for Trinity. After all, the minister seems to be hiding behind the unemployed in denying the principle that has been put forward by the hon. member for Trinity. Supply-Labour
stick to it. Maybe this advertising will help the unemployed and may create jobs, but if you have a principle you are going to stick to it. At least, I feel that seems to be the line of the hon. member for Trinity.

If I may intervene on a point of order, I think the hon. member for Timmins spoke on making his motion, and now he is speaking again. Under the rules there should be an intervening speaker before the hon. member rises again.
On that point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Timmins.

It is true I did have a few minutes to discuss this particular bill which appears to be sponsored in this house by the Social Credit wing of the Conservative party, the hon. members for Bow River, Acadia, and Jasper-Edson and others. As I pointed out the other day, I do not know just why they should be doing this. They seem to be contravening the policy of their party and the policy of their leader. Certainly, they are flying in the face of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
However, during the period when this bill has been debated, they have sought to create the impression in this house that everyone in Alberta is behind this bill, that support for it is unanimous, and that the measure is being held up by a bunch of irresponsible people. That is very far from being the truth, and I should like to point out something which will completely refute this effort to try to fool the house in this regard. I have here a copy of the Calgary Herald dated Thursday, January 19, which contains some very pertinent comments relating to this debate. I should like to quote briefly from these remarks. The newspaper states:
Mr. Harold Winch, C.C.F., M.P., quite rightly raised the question of national interest in the matter of a company seeking incorporation of a pipe-line operation when the subject came before the House of Commons Tuesday.
The points which he raised are certainly points significant in the over-all question of Canadian participation in development of its own resources. Surely there is no better place than the house to air the matter.
This is exactly what the members of this party have been trying to do in this regard assisted to a great extent, I hasten to add, by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who seems to be under no illusion whatsoever with regard to this bill. The article goes on to say:
Mr. Winch performed a service by pointing out that the bill would incorporate Aurora Pipeline Company, owned by Hudson Bay Gas and Oil Company of Calgary, which is in turn owned 68 per cent by the Continental Oil Company Limited, a United States corporation.
Mr. Winch pointed out that a Canadian company. Foothills Pipeline Company Limited, a subsidiary of Canadian-owned Pembina Pipeline Limited, is also seeking permission to export the by-products, although not by the same route or with the same objectives as Aurora.

The article continues:
"Serious consideration" should be given to whether the Aurora incorporation would benefit Alberta, he declared. And, certainly, that should be a consideration of the House of Commons.
This is something that we in this group have pointed out on more than one occasion. We have always been held up to scorn in doing so by the social credit wing of the Conservative party. They have attempted to lead us to believe that the bill is very definitely in the interest of, and has the support of the whole of the province of Alberta.
This article continues as follows:
The opportunity for Canadian participation and a considerable measure of control by a Canadian company is provided for in the Foothills proposal. It is a consideration to which these bodies must give the greatest weight.
The hon. member for Vancouver South pointed out very clearly that this bill in its present form is a complete negation of the policy that has been expounded by the Prime Minister and the Conservative party, and that it is something to which parliament should certainly give more consideration. We have been told not to bother in this regard. It has been suggested that after all there are fuel boards, both national and provincial, which will look after these details. The article appearing in the Calgary Herald has reference in this regard. It reads as follows:
The boards have the facilities and the personnel able to assess the technical aspects of all proposals. But a strictly technical view is not enough in itself. The Canadian view must also be taken and, for putting it forth in the house, Mr. Winch should be thanked. His fellow members would do well to have that view in mind.
One of the important objections to this bill is the fact that this Canadian view regarding the development of Canadian resources is completely forgotten.
Oil and gas represent a most valuable and important resource which this country possesses. The rank and file of Canadians across this country, who are the consumers of these resources, have been gouged very severely as a result of the sell-out of these resources to particular interests in this field of production. We saw an example of this in the pipe line debate of 1956. Fortunes were made by a few individuals at that time, of course, the consumers, of this and future generations, must bear the cost of providing these fortunes. An unnecessary amount of money has been written into the cost of selling these products for the benefit of a few privileged individuals, and this is the type of thing we in this country can well do without, in respect of our natural resources. In order to avoid further sell-outs of this type, which result in the loss of thousands of dollars, we should be more careful in the future than we have been in the past.

Those hon. members on the government side of this chamber, who apparently are in favour of this bill, should heed the words of one of the ministers of the crown, and I refer to the present Minister of Agriculture, who was the former minister of northern affairs and national resources. What he has said in the past in regard to our natural resources I think is very appropriate at this time during the discussion of this bill.
I would like to refer to some of his remarks which can be found at page 3323 of Hansard of August 9, 1958, in a speech which I made at that time. He is quoted there as follows:
To be very blunt about it, If you go back to the experience of the second world war you will find that the American government was very much concerned about the rapid depletion of their strategic resources and there was set up a presidential committee in that country to examine into this matter. This committee reported in 1952 and their report is known as the Paley report. The Paley report says in plain English that the resources of the United States of America are not unlimited and that, at the present time, they are in a deficit position so far as total resources are concerned to maintain their industrial economy. Naturally they have to seek out reserves both of energy and mineral resources in every land.
We have seen examples of their seeking out of these resources, unfortunately to our sorrow, on more than one occasion.
The minister had more to say in this regard which is becoming more pertinent as time goes on. He is reported on the same page as follows:
-we are the nation on the northern half of this continent and we want to make certain that the interests, not only of the present generation, are protected, but that the interests of generations unborn will also be preserved.
I think those remarks are exactly in line with what hon. members of this group have said in regard to this measure and other similar measures.
At the same page the minister is quoted further as follows:
We in Canada, whether because an act of grace, or because of our geographical location, or simply as a result of inertia, have not had our resources depleted so widely as the American resources have been depleted, without plan.
That again is something completely in line with the stand we are taking. Here we have a minister of the crown agreeing completely with this group in this regard but still we have this bill being promoted at this time by certain member of the government side of this chamber.
From the same source I repeat the following quotation:
We may have, either by the grace of God, or by our own inertia, been saved from having misused our resources.

I cannot help but wonder at the thinking and inconsistency of hon. members on the government side when some of them, as the minister, recognize this problem, while others insist on blindly promoting and executing the things condemned in the words of the minister.
Beginning on the same page and carrying over to the next, the minister is further quoted as follows:
It is simply that we have a determination to avoid these mistakes, if possible, in our country in relation to the future development and efficient use of those resources.
Does this bill represent an example of that determination to avoid these mistakes in the future? Is this the way the government intends to avoid making these mistakes, which the hon. minister recognized as having been made before, the depletion, waste and squandering of the resources in the country to the south? I suggest by the passage of this bill we will be encouraging those individuals to come in and do the same in this country, regarding our natural resources, as they have done in regard to their own.
The Minister of Agriculture, the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, had more to say regarding this subject. He is quoted at page 3324 of Hansard of August 9, 1958 as follows:
Because we have great reserves of minerals of all kinds, Canada is a great centre of interest in an economico-political way. For that reason, some consideration and logic had to come in respect of exploitation of these resources.
I would like to heartily endorse the words of the minister in this respect and suggest that it is about time we had some logic regarding these resources. I fail to see the existence of logic in the bill that is presently before us.
Later on the same day, the minister is quoted as saying:
-there is no use in doing all this work if there is not some thought given to a long range conservation concept of the most efficient use of those resources.
The hon. member for Timiskaming has pointed out the need for developing secondary industries and using those resources to build our own country into something other than a country producing primary products. If we are to avoid becoming hewers of wood and drawers of water, something to which the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet have referred from coast to coast in this country, then certainly we cannot endorse bills of this kind.
Finally, the minister went on to say:
I want to make it clear that unless we formulate a plan for the use of our resources we may lose the long range strategic necessity of having control of those resources in our hands,-

How true, Mr. Chairman. I continue:
-either for world use, or for people over the world, or most effective use in the North American economic picture.
Well, maybe this particular bill would fit in the North American economic picture but certainly it will not fit into the Canadian picture. If hon. members on the government side cannot agree with the C.C.F. that in a matter of this kind we should consider the benefit to Canadians as a whole, then surely they should listen to their own minister and his plea to try to avoid the mistakes of the past. If they cannot agree with the so-called policy of the Prime Minister and of the members of the Tory party, how do they expect the people are going to believe the Prime Minister at all if he rises in his place and expounds one view and then members of his party advocate a bill that is exactly the opposite to what he expounds?
The hon. member does not know what he is talking about.
I wish the hon. member who made that interjection would rise in his place and tell us what he is talking about.

On that very point, I am talking about the fact that this company wishes to export a product which is gasoline. The company said that 90 per cent of the product they wished to export is gasoline. This is a product that we have a surplus of in western Canada. How we can develop further industry out of gasoline is beyond my comprehension. If the hon. member looked at it in that light he would probably agree with me. If the hon. member says it is not gasoline, why did not the hon. member of his party in the committee question the statement of the representative of the Hudson's Bay Gas and Oil Company who said in the committee that it was gasoline?

We seem to be learning more about this bill all the time. During the discussion of this bill we have had a difficult time eliciting any information at all. First of all, no record was kept of the committee meetings in the other place-
This information is on the records of the committee. Read the record.

On a point of order, may I draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that there is one vocal member on the other side who has not the courtesy to rise before he speaks. I wonder whether you would draw the rule to his attention.
